notes:
Nuclear Basics

  • Nucleus: $Z$ protons + $N$ neutrons; mass number $A = Z+N$. Nuclear radius $R = R_0A^{1/3}$, $R_0 = 1.2$ fm; nuclear density is constant ($\approx 2.3\times10^{17}\ \text{kg/m}^3$) for all nuclei.
  • Isotopes: same $Z$, different $A$. Isobars: same $A$, different $Z$. Isotones: same $N$.

Mass-Energy & Binding Energy

  • Mass defect $\Delta m = [Zm_p + Nm_n] - M_{nucleus}$. Binding energy $BE = \Delta m\,c^2$ (1 u $= 931.5$ MeV).
  • Binding energy per nucleon $BE/A$ is a measure of stability; it rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks (~8.7 MeV) near $A\approx56$ (iron), then slowly falls for heavy nuclei — this shape explains both fusion (light nuclei) and fission (heavy nuclei) releasing energy, since both move nuclei towards the peak.

Radioactivity

  • Decay law: $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, activity $A = \lambda N$, SI unit becquerel (Bq); 1 curie $= 3.7\times10^{10}$ Bq.
  • Half-life $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$. Mean life $\tau = 1/\lambda = T_{1/2}/0.693 = 1.44\,T_{1/2}$.
  • After $n$ half-lives, fraction remaining $= (1/2)^n$.

Fission & Fusion

  • Fission: heavy nucleus (e.g. $^{235}_{92}\text{U}$) splits into two medium nuclei + neutrons, releasing ~200 MeV; basis of nuclear reactors (chain reaction, controlled by moderators/control rods).
  • Fusion: light nuclei combine (e.g. proton-proton cycle in the Sun) releasing energy; requires extremely high temperature to overcome Coulomb repulsion.

Exam tip

KCET typically asks 2 questions: one numerical on radioactive decay/half-life, and one on binding energy per nucleon or mass defect. Know 1 u = 931.5 MeV by heart.

questions.q: The radius of a nucleus with mass number 64 compared to one with mass number 8 is
A radioactive sample has a half-life of 20 days. The fraction of the sample remaining after 60 days is
questions.explanation: 60 days $= 3$ half-lives; fraction remaining $= (1/2)^3 = 1/8$.

questions.q: The binding energy per nucleon is maximum for nuclei with mass number around
questions.explanation: The BE/A curve peaks near $A \approx 56$ (iron group), which is why iron-group nuclei are the most stable.

questions.q: In beta-minus decay, a nucleus transforms as
options: only a gamma photon is emitted
a neutron converts to a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino
a proton converts to a neutron, emitting a positron
questions.explanation: $\beta^-$ decay: $n \to p + e^- + \bar{\nu}$; the atomic number increases by 1 while mass number stays the same.

questions.q: 1 atomic mass unit (u) is equivalent to an energy of
questions.explanation: By $E = \Delta m c^2$, 1 u $= 1.66\times10^{-27}$ kg corresponds to 931.5 MeV.

questions.q: The activity of a radioactive sample is 8000 disintegrations per second initially. After two half-lives, the activity becomes
questions.explanation: Activity halves every half-life: after 2 half-lives, $8000\times(1/2)^2 = 2000$ dps.

questions.q: The mean life $\tau$ of a radioactive substance is related to its half-life $T_{1/2}$ by
In nuclear fission of $^{235}_{92}\text{U}$, energy is released because
options: the binding energy per nucleon of products is less than that of uranium
the binding energy per nucleon of products is greater than that of uranium
questions.explanation: Fission products (medium mass number) lie closer to the peak of the BE/A curve, so they are more tightly bound per nucleon than uranium; this difference in BE/A, multiplied by $A$, appears as released energy.

questions.q: A nucleus $^{A}_{Z}X$ emits one alpha particle followed by one beta-minus particle. The resulting nucleus is
questions.explanation: Alpha emission: $Z\to Z-2$, $A\to A-4$. Beta-minus emission: $Z\to Z-1$ (mass number unchanged). Net: $A-4$, $Z-2+1 = Z-1$.

questions.q: The density of nuclear matter
options: is approximately the same for all nuclei
questions.explanation: Since $R\propto A^{1/3}$, volume $\propto A$, and mass $\propto A$, so density (mass/volume) is nearly constant, independent of $A$, for all nuclei.

questions.q: A sample initially contains $N_0$ radioactive nuclei. The number of nuclei that have decayed after a time equal to its mean life $\tau$ is approximately
questions.explanation: $N = N_0e^{-\lambda\tau} = N_0e^{-1} \approx 0.37N_0$ remain, so decayed fraction $= N_0 - 0.37N_0 = 0.63N_0$.

questions.q: Two nuclei have mass numbers in the ratio 1:8. The ratio of their nuclear radii is
The mass defect of a nucleus refers to
options: the mass of the electron cloud
the loss of mass number during fission
the difference between the mass of the nucleus and the sum of masses of its free constituent nucleons
the mass lost due to radioactive decay
questions.explanation: Mass defect $\Delta m = Zm_p + Nm_n - M_{nucleus}$; this 'missing' mass appears as the binding energy holding the nucleus together.

questions.q: In a nuclear reactor, control rods (e.g. cadmium or boron) are used to
options: absorb excess neutrons and control the chain reaction
questions.explanation: Control rods absorb neutrons, allowing the number of neutrons causing further fission to be regulated so the chain reaction proceeds at a steady, controlled rate.

questions.q: The energy released in the fusion of light nuclei (e.g. in the Sun) occurs because
options: the binding energy per nucleon increases as lighter nuclei combine into a more tightly bound nucleus
the binding energy per nucleon decreases
neutrons are absorbed without any change in binding energy
questions.explanation: Combining light nuclei (low BE/A) into a heavier nucleus (higher BE/A, closer to the peak) releases the difference in binding energy as energy.

questions.q: A radioactive nuclide has decay constant $\lambda = 0.0231\ \text{day}^{-1}$. Its half-life is approximately
Isotopes of an element have
options: the same mass number but different atomic number
the same number of protons but different number of neutrons
the same number of neutrons but different number of protons
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same $Z$ (proton number, hence same chemical properties) but different $N$ (neutron number), so different mass number $A$.

questions.q: If the half-life of a radioactive element is $T$, the time taken for 87.5% of the sample to decay is
questions.explanation: 87.5% decayed means 12.5% $= 1/8$ remains $= (1/2)^3$, which takes 3 half-lives, i.e. $3T$.

questions.q: The SI unit of radioactive activity is the
questions.explanation: The becquerel (Bq), defined as one disintegration per second, is the SI unit of activity; the curie is an older, non-SI unit.

questions.q: An activity of $3.7\times10^{10}$ Bq is equal to
questions.explanation: By definition, 1 curie $= 3.7\times10^{10}$ Bq, so this activity equals exactly 1 Ci.

questions.q: During gamma decay of a nucleus, the mass number and atomic number
options: A decreases by 4, Z decreases by 2
Z increases by 1, A stays unchanged
questions.explanation: Gamma decay is simply the emission of a high-energy photon as an excited nucleus drops to a lower energy state; no particle is ejected, so $A$ and $Z$ are both unchanged.

questions.q: In the radioactive decay chain from $^{238}_{92}\text{U}$ to the stable nucleus $^{206}_{82}\text{Pb}$, the number of alpha and beta particles emitted are respectively
questions.explanation: Mass number drops by $238-206=32$, requiring $32/4=8$ alpha particles, which alone would drop $Z$ by 16 (to 76). To reach $Z=82$, 6 beta particles (each raising $Z$ by 1) are also needed.

questions.q: The binding energy of a deuteron ($^2_1\text{H}$, mass 2.014102 u), given $m_p = 1.007825$ u and $m_n = 1.008665$ u, is close to
The nuclear force between nucleons is best described as
options: obeying an inverse-square law, like the Coulomb force
questions.explanation: The nuclear (strong) force acts only over very short distances (a few fm), is much stronger than the Coulomb force at those distances, and acts equally between proton-proton, neutron-neutron, and proton-neutron pairs (charge-independent).

questions.q: Isobars are nuclei that have
options: the same neutron number, different atomic numbers
the same mass number, different atomic numbers
the same number of protons and neutrons
the same atomic number, different mass numbers
questions.explanation: Isobars share the same mass number $A$ but differ in atomic number $Z$ (and hence in the number of protons and neutrons); this is distinct from isotopes, which share the same $Z$.

questions.q: A radioactive sample decays for a time equal to twice its mean life ($t=2\tau$). The fraction of the original sample remaining is approximately
questions.explanation: $N/N_0 = e^{-t/\tau} = e^{-2} \approx 0.135$, i.e. about 13.5% remains.

questions.q: The energy released in the fission of a single $^{235}_{92}\text{U}$ nucleus is approximately
questions.explanation: Fission of one uranium-235 nucleus typically releases about 200 MeV of energy, most of it as kinetic energy of the fission fragments.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly ranks the penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation from LEAST to MOST penetrating?
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are stopped by paper/skin, beta particles need a few mm of aluminium, while gamma rays require thick lead or concrete; so penetrating power increases as alpha < beta < gamma.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly ranks the ionising power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation from MOST to LEAST?
questions.explanation: Alpha particles, being heavy and doubly charged, ionise matter most strongly over a short path; gamma rays, being uncharged and highly penetrating, ionise the least per unit path length. Order: alpha > beta > gamma.

questions.q: A radioactive sample decays such that $N/N_0 = 1/e^2$ after time $t$. The value of $\lambda t$ is
questions.explanation: $N/N_0 = e^{-\lambda t} = e^{-2} \Rightarrow \lambda t = 2$.

questions.q: The half-life of a given radioactive nuclide is determined by
options: the nature of the nuclide (its decay constant $\lambda$)
the physical state (solid, liquid or gas)
questions.explanation: Half-life $T_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda$ depends only on the decay constant, a fixed property of the particular nuclide, and is unaffected by the quantity present or by external physical/chemical conditions.

questions.q: The SI unit of the radioactive decay constant $\lambda$ is
questions.explanation: From $N=N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, the exponent must be dimensionless, so $\lambda$ has units of inverse time, i.e. $s^{-1}$.

questions.q: Two radioactive samples A and B, starting with equal numbers of nuclei, have half-lives $T$ and $2T$ respectively. After a time $2T$, the ratio of undecayed nuclei $N_A:N_B$ is
questions.explanation: In time $2T$, sample A completes 2 half-lives, so $N_A = N_0/4$; sample B completes 1 half-life, so $N_B = N_0/2$. Ratio $N_A:N_B = (1/4):(1/2) = 1:2$.

questions.q: The process in which a heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei with the release of energy is called
questions.explanation: Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus (e.g. uranium-235) into two medium-mass fragments, releasing a large amount of energy along with a few neutrons.

questions.q: For nuclear fusion to occur between two light nuclei, extremely high temperatures are required mainly to
options: reduce the binding energy of the nuclei
increase the mass of the nuclei
overcome the strong mutual Coulomb repulsion between the positively charged nuclei so they can get close enough for the nuclear force to act
questions.explanation: Two positively charged nuclei repel each other electrostatically; only at extremely high temperatures do they gain enough kinetic energy to overcome this repulsion and approach close enough (about a few fm) for the short-range nuclear force to bind them.

questions.q: A nucleus of mass number 240 (binding energy per nucleon 7.6 MeV) splits into two fragments with a combined mass number of 240 and an average binding energy per nucleon of about 8.5 MeV. The approximate energy released per fission event is
questions.explanation: Total binding energy before $\approx 240\times7.6 = 1824$ MeV; after $\approx 240\times8.5 = 2040$ MeV. Energy released $\approx 2040-1824 = 216$ MeV.

questions.q: A self-sustained chain reaction in a nuclear reactor is maintained when the neutron multiplication factor $k$ equals
questions.explanation: When $k=1$ (critical), the number of neutrons causing fission in successive generations stays constant, sustaining a steady chain reaction; $k<1$ is subcritical (reaction dies out) and $k>1$ is supercritical (reaction grows uncontrollably).

questions.q: Which of the following statements about radioactive decay is correct?
options: It can be sped up by heating the sample
It always produces only gamma rays
It is a statistical (random) process, unaffected by external conditions like temperature or pressure
It depends strongly on the chemical compound the radioactive atom is part of
questions.explanation: Radioactive decay is a spontaneous, random nuclear process; the decay constant is unaffected by temperature, pressure, or the chemical environment of the atom.

questions.q: The mass defect of a helium-4 nucleus is 0.0304 u (using $m_p=1.007825$ u, $m_n=1.008665$ u). Its binding energy per nucleon is approximately
questions.explanation: Total binding energy $= 0.0304\times931.5 \approx 28.3$ MeV; per nucleon (A=4), $BE/A \approx 28.3/4 \approx 7.1$ MeV.

questions.q: In any nuclear reaction, the quantities that are always conserved include
options: only atomic number, not mass number
questions.explanation: In every nuclear reaction, the total mass number (nucleon number) and total charge (sum of atomic numbers) on both sides must balance, even though total rest mass and kinetic energy can be interconverted.
